Chapter Six: The Art of Living with Awareness
You know, there’s this subtle difference between just going through the motions and actually being awake to what’s happening right now. Think about it—most days, routines kind of take over. There’s the blaring morning alarm, the usual commute, endless meetings, and a list of chores that never seems to end.
It’s so easy to slip into that autopilot mode, isn’t it? Hours can pass, and you barely notice. But every once in a while, something snaps you out of it—maybe a sudden fit of laughter, the taste of your favorite meal, or just the way sunlight spills across your kitchen table. In those moments, everything feels sharper, more alive.
I remember a neighbor sharing how, after years of rushing through her days, she decided to try something different. She started really paying attention. At first, it was just little things—pausing to feel the warmth of her coffee mug, listening to her child’s footsteps, noticing her own breath.
She told me it felt a bit awkward at first, maybe even pointless. But slowly, something changed. The ordinary started to feel, well, extraordinary. She felt more present, less anxious, and way more connected to the people around her.
See, living with awareness isn’t about doing it perfectly, or being mindful every single second. It’s about coming back to the present, over and over again. Most of us don’t realize just how much of life we miss when our attention’s scattered. The mind either jumps ahead to worries about the future, or drifts back to old regrets. Rarely does it settle in the now.
But here’s the thing—when you bring awareness to even the simplest moments, life starts to feel richer.
I have a friend who was totally overwhelmed by work. He started taking daily walks—not to plan or problem-solve, but just to notice things. The changing colors of the trees, the steady rhythm of his steps, the feel of cool air on his face. These little acts of attention became anchors for him, offering a sense of calm that helped him handle stress a lot better.
What he learned—and what so many of us discover—is that awareness isn’t something you achieve once and for all. It’s a way of being. It’s about noticing what’s here, right now, without judgment or trying to push things away.
A lot of people fall into the trap of believing happiness is always somewhere in the future, just out of reach, waiting after that next big accomplishment. But really, life’s happening right here, in every breath and every heartbeat.
One parent told me, after years of multitasking, that the moments with their kids they remembered most were the ones where they were fully present—listening, laughing, just being together. Those moments, even though they were brief, left the deepest mark.
Living with awareness is a practice, not some final destination. It takes patience, a bit of curiosity, and a willingness to start over, moment by moment. Most people don’t realize just how much peace there is when you stop trying to control everything and simply pay attention to what’s right in front of you.
